essay_title: Mixed Feelings in Jane Austen's Sense and Sensibility

outline.summary: Mixed feelings are at the heart of Sense and Sensibility. The intuitive 'recipe' or 'disequilibrium' model — two parts gratitude + one part happiness + a dash of resentment = an Elinor — poorly serves the novel. That recipe descends from Galen's humours tradition (n.1: Paster, Humoring the Body). In fact mixed feelings are 'a matter of negotiated circumstances where feelings may be at odds as they converge on character.' The chapter offers a rhetorical-situated alternative drawing on Barsalou + Barrett's situated emotion and on Kahneman's behavioral economics, opposed both to the Galenic disequilibrium model and to the Cognitive Approaches to Literature program (theory-of-mind reading).

Title foregrounds the arc of two characters as they mutually modify toward a happy ending. Austen's 'utilitarian concern' calculates feelings 'mixed at the novel's midpoint between emotional states more stable' (n.2: distinguishes Damasio's emotion/feeling split; Massumi's sociolinguistic-fixing; Brian Massumi's Parables for the Virtual; Gross's own Secret History of Emotion 2006).

A muscle-based talking head from a 2005 Virtual Reality article (Fig. 4.1) illustrates a visual midpoint calculation by blending algorithm; the middle images are uncanny because mathematically unhinged from humanity (n.3: Wired uncanny-valley; Mori; sorites-paradox argument).

The Dashwood women open 'settled' in Sussex and end 'happily resettled' in Barton and Delaford where 'strong family affection' is easily communicated (Austen p.289). The folk-psychological formula EMOTIONAL STABILITY → MIXED FEELINGS → EMOTIONAL STABILITY underlies idioms like 'I FEEL NOT HALF BAD' and 'I HAVE HALF A MIND TO...' — aposiopesis (n.4: text uses Oxford World's Classics S&S ed. Kinsley/Doody/Lamont 2008).

Half-mind idioms confirm 'I FEEL TORN' is conceptual blending (Fauconnier & Turner, n.6). 'We still live in the wake of a general utilitarianism famously articulated by Jeremy Bentham just before Austen drafted in the 1790s a precursor epistolary novel "Elinor and Marianne"' (n.7: Bernanke hedonics; McCloskey critique). 'For the crass utilitarian, emotion, and most importantly happiness, can be quantified and therefore halved.'

'But who wants to be a crass utilitarian? Certainly not Jeremy Bentham' (n.8: Mill's Bentham + Coleridge synthesis). Fewer than one might think; pre-calculation fog is heavy. The alternative: 'mixed feelings materialize in reference values that are negotiated only by way of rhetoric.'

Pixar aesthetics, blending algorithms. Ekman's 'basic emotions' (n.9: Ekman 1992 'An Argument for Basic Emotions') treat non-basic emotions as 'combinations of the basic emotions, which may be called blends or mixed emotional states' (e.g. smug = enjoyment + contempt), with the caveat that what we perceive as mixed is likely basic emotions passing in microseconds. Against this, Austen's emotional rhetoric will appear 'quaint, wordy, and relatively obscure' — but is in fact newly evident from a post-utilitarian standpoint.

outline.function: the key scene introduced — Vol. III Elinor/Edward
outline.summary: The key Sense and Sensibility scene: in the final Volume III, Elinor — in reciprocal love with unavailable Edward — must inform him that his languishing engagement to rival Lucy might now be realized since Colonel Brandon has promised him a small rectory.

Edward appears suddenly on the scene. Elinor 'astonished' (n.10: Austen p.213 has 'Elinor's astonishment at this commission from Colonel Brandon') and 'particularly uncomfortable for some minutes' (Austen p.217). She reports with irony the £200 per annum that might just establish 'all his views of happiness' (Austen p.218) — including his marriage to Lucy. The narrator: 'What Edward felt, as he could not say it himself, it cannot be expected that anyone else should say for him. He looked all the astonishment which such unexpected, such unthought-of information could not fail of exciting; but he said only these two words: "Colonel Brandon!"'

First, against Zunshine + Vermeule (mind-reading literary critics), Edward's legibility is denied externally AND internally — narrator says Edward could not say it to himself. Second, against Marianne and other calculating externalists who look to physiognomy for truths, Edward's expression refers only to 'absence at the heart, but not apathy.' Third, the physiognomist sees only 'astonishment' (Fig. 4.2 — Pride and Prejudice illustration), 'in its unadulterated form, nothing will change per se, or what the narrator calls excitement.' Like the muscle-based talking head, canonic representations of astonishment (n.11: Charles Le Brun) incorporate the scalar inflection admiration and fear (Fig. 4.3 — Le Brun Astonishment-with-Fear + Admiration-with-Astonishment).

The 1833 Pride and Prejudice astonishment illustration relies fundamentally on context (Mr. Bennet's trepidation about Darcy now unviable because Darcy saved Lydia). 'Indeed this moment is awkward in the most profound sense because it destabilizes the emotional arc in both temporal directions as the focal characters, and we as readers, must revise feelings already felt.' Astonishment (or 'surprise', n.12 OED etymology — astonare 'strike with thunderbolt') renders any calculation difficult, since it's only a common denominator: 'fear over surprise, admiration over surprise...' through six 'brief and episodic' emotions Ekman distinguishes from enduring 'affective commitments' (n.13).

Scientists confront this in lab: response phenomenon registers historically as 'attention,' 'excitement,' or 'surprise.' Jerome Kagan (n.14: Kagan 2007 What Is Emotion?; Daniel Dror on excitement) cites gender study where subjects took longer judging fearful men's faces (atypical). Kagan urges thinking incentive/brain in terms of response-uncertainty, not stereotyped incentive-response matching. Astonishment in Austen 'obscures precisely because it is reflexive and all too predictable.'

outline.function: anti-skepticism — Austen withholds omniscience but story proceeds
outline.summary: Would a 'God's eye perspective, advanced measurement, or airtight evolutionary psychology' allow us to read Edward's mixed feelings as a real human being (n.15: Alex Woloch The One vs. the Many)? No — Austen frustrates omniscient narration. Yet the story proceeds — and Ryle (n.16: Ryle 'Jane Austen and the Moralists' 1966; MacIntyre After Virtue; Austen-as-Aristotelian thesis: 'when Jane Austen speaks of happiness, she does so as an Aristotelian'; McCloskey Bourgeois Virtues) and McIntyre read Austen as a narrator of emotional equilibrium. **GROSS DEPARTS:** 'Austenian happiness is not Aristotelian + Christian, as MacIntyre suggests' (n.16). Story proceeds by mixed feelings understood against Ekman.

Barsalou, Barrett, and colleagues' 2011 Neuropsychologia article 'Grounding Emotion in Situated Conceptualization' renders Kagan's uncertainty problem productive: catch-trials separate the emotional incentive from its conceptualization (n.17: Ollinger et al. on catch-trial method). Fig. 4.4: Senator Jim Webb's face — angry in (a), elated in (b) when situated. The 'emotion paradox': automatic perception of Webb as angry-or-elated 'depending upon the image, even though sufficient information for this judgment is not unambiguously displayed on his face or body' (n.18: Barrett, Lindquist, Gendron 2007 'Language as Context for Emotional Perception'). Emotions are not stereotyped triggered brain mechanisms but situated.

Barrett/Barsalou test situated emotion where situations themselves are ambiguous. Quote Knight Dunlap 1932 (n.19 'Are Emotions Teleological Constructs?'): 'I may apprehend my situation primarily as one in which my welfare is threatened. I call my inner responses fear. You may apprehend my situation as one in which I fight against the threat; you say I am angry. Which is correct? The answer may be: Both!' Fear of runner lost on wooded trail differs from fear of unprepared presenter — agent conceptualizes situations differently and mobilizes different brain regions (social fear: left dorsolateral PFC + inferior frontal gyrus, executive control not motor; physical fear: motor regions, 'wheels spinning vs. legs moving').

Experiment proceeds 'in a manner that speaks to the literary humanities and especially the art of rhetoric' (n.20: Griffiths + Scarantino 'emotions in the wild'). Block-quoted protocol: participants 'immerse' in situations from first-person (Gross notes: actually written second-person, raising literary-rhetorical questions of identification — n.21 Beth Innocenti on Cicero's 'Verrine' vivid description / vivacity; n.22 'Grounding Emotion' supplementary materials). Wittgensteinian core-less concepts (a 'game' has no core but prototypes).

outline.function: scan protocol + Creative Writing 101 + dinner-party scenario
outline.summary: Scan protocol: 30 physical-danger / 30 social-evaluation core situations mixed; participants rate how easily they experience each of four concepts (anger, fear, observe, plan). Conclusion: 'specific instances of emotion are constructed dynamically within neural circuitry distributed across the brain to represent an emotion in a particular situation.' Mini-narratives' protocols are like 'Creative Writing 101.' Gross constructs the dinner-party scenario: contentious-debate uncomfortable silence chest-tightening; angry-at-self or fearful-of-distance depends on situation including 'interested onlookers.'

outline.function: Austen's critique of utilitarianism reframed via interested-onlookers — CHAPTER ARGUMENTATIVE CRUX
outline.summary: 'Now returning to Austen's critique of utilitarianism, my mixed feelings would be determined not by any predictable calculation but rather in dynamic relationship with onlookers who might in fact be extrinsic.' Recall the Edward astonishment scene: utilitarian efforts as readers are explicitly frustrated. Although Elinor is implicated by Edward's 'look' only she could grant at that moment, 'anyone' — including the reader — is denied the emotional label; Elinor and we as 'happiness calculators' are disabled.

outline.function: interested-onlookers definition + Lucy's secret calculation (Austen p.221)
outline.summary: 'The entire scene is framed by a mockery of utilitarian calculation that would have all Edward's views of happiness realized by a sum lying somewhere between £200 and x = the availability of Colonel Brandon's servants, carriage, cows, and poultry, as "secretly" calculated by Lucy in the following scene' (Austen p.221). **DEFINITION:** 'In light of Barrett and Barsalou, we can say that Edward's mixed feelings are defined by interested onlookers who, in this case, include us.'

outline.function: Elinor's disingenuous expected-utility frame (Austen p.198) + Marianne's relative-value retort
outline.summary: 'Disingenuously (198), Elinor earlier explains the situation to Marianne in terms of what we now call "expected utility" that rationally calculates absolute value: "Edward will marry Lucy; he will marry a woman superior in person and understanding to half her sex; and time and habit will teach him to forget that he ever thought another superior to her."' Looking ahead to Kahneman-Tversky, Marianne offers a critique of expected utility by addressing Elinor as 'a non-abstract and unaveraged person who should be interested not in absolute value, but in her own relative superiority to Lucy': 'If such is your way of thinking, replies Marianne, if the loss of what is most valued is so easily to be made up by something else, your resolution, your self-command, are, perhaps, a little less to be wondered at.' This is Marianne's anti-utilitarian critique grounded in relative value.

**KEY RHETORICAL DEVICE:** 'Not no feelings, to use the double negative Austen found so stylistically congenial.' Mixed feelings 'tempt us to read along with astonishment, excitement, gratitude, and happiness, perhaps also love, regret, shame, unhappiness, disgust, terror, melancholy, and we could go on like Elinor who finally sits down to "reconsider the past, recall the words and endeavour to comprehend all the feelings of Edward; and, of course, to reflect on her own with discontent"' (Austen p.219). 'Thus our analysis proceeds not despite, but precisely because of the mixed feelings that Austen treats masterfully when considered from this perspective of recent cognitive science and post-utilitarian psychology.' Pivot to Kahneman's 'Reference Points, Anchors, Norms, and Mixed Feelings' (n.24: Kahneman 1992 Org Behavior & Human Decision Processes; n.23: Booth on Emma; van Soni Mourning Happiness).

outline.function: Kahneman on mixed feelings as ambivalencies
outline.summary: 'Explicitly for Kahneman, mixed feelings are not calculable intermediates but rather ambivalencies that reference multiple points subject to what he calls, depending upon the example, negotiation or persuasion.' Example: $5000-expected raise, $3000-received raise — psychological value coded as gain (vs. zero) or loss (vs. $5000); 'any raise of less than $5000 is experienced both as a gain and as a loss, at different times' (Kahneman p.306).

Mixed feelings in judgment tasks are irresolvable with reference to single composites or fixed temporality; Kahneman would not be impressed by blending algorithms. Bentham himself qualified absolute-value models (n.25: Bentham Fragment 1776, Introduction 1780, Burns 'Happiness and Utility' 2005): he was deeply interested in 'circumstances influencing sensibility' (gender, education, rank) — 'Caeteris paribus the quantum of sensibility appears to be greater in the higher ranks of men than in the lower'; redesigned law/government around historically specific biases. Reference values via expectation, negotiation, balance sheets (n.26: Bentham ch. VI 'Of Circumstances Influencing Sensibility').

outline.function: Kahneman's rhetoric of possibilities — focusing illusion
outline.summary: Negotiators, politicians, advertisers communicate reference points: labor unions lowball, politicians announce small initiatives with fanfare, advertisers exploit Kahneman's 'focusing illusion' (n.27: Schkade + Kahneman 'Does Living in California Make People Happy?' 1998). 'In a nutshell, Kahneman ties value to a rhetoric of possibilities.'

outline.function: paradiastole + Peacham + Skinner + Quentin Skinner objection
outline.summary: Sophistry / Plato's bad-rhetoric: paradiastole 'when the truth is opposed by false terms' (Renaissance rhetorician Henry Peacham). But Kahneman: skillful negotiator smoothes loss-aversion with alternative reference points (p.307) — 'I am not losing a vehicle, I am gaining freedom from debt,' 'Remember you are not losing a daughter — you are gaining a son.' Persuasion is 'inillimitable' because reference points are not fixed and subject to revision. Against Quentin Skinner's generic paradiastole account (n.28: 'in utramque partem, on either side'), 'Kahneman's example shows how reference values are lodged in a recalcitrant world subject, however, to negotiation.'

outline.function: duck-rabbit + qualitative core of quantitative model
outline.summary: Mixed feelings are 'inillimitable' but to identify/analyze/explain, we need relevant reference points producing a 'duck/rabbit effect' (n.29: Kahneman et al. on objective happiness in Well-Being). Feelings are mixed 'by way of concrete reference points that can be incorporated into a quantitative model. But the model is also qualitative at its core; by way of Kahneman's expectation, rhetoric constitutes the finite set of relationships that makes feeling quantifiable in the first place.'

outline.function: Kahneman's actual point + behavioral economics genealogy
outline.summary: Kahneman doesn't deem utilitarian models inherently misleading — they must account for psychology and the rhetorics shaping them. Behavioral economics emerges from rediscovering 'the rhetoric of economics' in Adam Smith (rhetoric + moral sentiments + wealth of nations integration; n.30: Hirschman Passions and the Interests 1977). Rhetoric is the expert domain for emotion and irrationalism.

outline.function: irrationalism returns to Edward — six reference points
outline.summary: Following Kahneman, Edward is the subject with multiple/conflicting reference points: (1) gratitude toward Brandon + Elinor enabling minimal happiness; (2) resentment toward Brandon + Elinor for disabling optimal happiness; (3) minimal obligation toward Lucy; (4) maximal obligation toward Elinor more recently wooed; (5) disgust with whomever including himself for the awkward situation; (6) specific astonishment that Elinor populated category 5 by throwing the awkward situation in his face.

outline.function: Elinor as interested-negotiator / skilled rhetorician / subtle seducer
outline.summary: Elinor is 'an interested negotiator, and we might call her a skilled rhetorician, even a very, very subtle seducer.' She has extracted gratitude without allowing he would owe her anything; confronted Edward with choice between lowered + raised expectations; exploited what Kahneman + Tversky famously call 'loss aversion' by presenting herself as the more immediate love object while articulating the very alienation that would force Edward's hand. 'No wonder Edward is not just specifically but also generally astonished.'

Mixed feelings depend on reference points outside any negotiator's control — at certain point the balance sheet 'is what it is.' Reading Austen we are reading literary fiction, but Kahneman's example also is 'a work of literary fiction... an imaginative mini-narrative populated not with real human beings but implied human beings for whom context never disappears completely into the depths of psyche. There is a way in which scenario building — even for oneself — always relies upon narrative fictionality.' Context matters fundamentally; Kahneman's social science and Austen's fiction are 'different but compatibly insightful.'

outline.function: Goring's Rhetoric of Sensibility + sentimental fiction's witnessed eloquence
outline.summary: Paul Goring's The Rhetoric of Sensibility in Eighteenth-Century Culture (n.31: Cambridge 2005) reminds us the question extends to sentimental novel's embedding genre — Richardson's Pamela, Fielding's David Simple, McKenzie's Man of Feeling, Sterne's Sentimental Journey. Sentimental fiction's rhetoric of emotion depends 'fundamentally not just upon the conventions of emotional expression à la Lavater (in our day Ekman) but rather upon scene mechanics, including the staging of witnessed eloquence that implicates a reader' (Goring p.153). 'Emotional mechanics of the scene' materialize in negotiated reference values (n.32: Hume on counterfactuals; Hart + Honoré on cause/condition relativity).

By way of conclusion, focus on the role of gossips John Dashwood and Mrs. Jennings, who allow Austen to establish reference points — 'Kahnemanite norms' — outside the central characters' immediate purview. Epigraphic: Barrett's article on 'top-down' visual impact of gossip (Fig. 4.5). Kahneman + Miller's 1986 'Norm Theory: Comparing Reality to Its Alternatives' cites Barsalou on rejecting normality-as-formal-probability, offering instead 'phenomenology of surprise' (n.33). PERCEIVED ABNORMALITY → sympathy (imaginary victim injured during robbery only because regular store closed for renovations); AVAILABILITY OF COUNTERFACTUALS → sympathy (5-min plane-miss vs. 30-min plane-miss). Victims lose sympathy when ACTIONS OF FOCAL INDIVIDUAL mutable vs. background actors — 'blame the victim.'

outline.function: John Dashwood, Mrs. Jennings, Edward-Lucy engagement family-loyalty framing
outline.summary: John Dashwood situates Edward's engagement to Lucy in family loyalty: 'Duty, affection, and everything was disregarded. I never thought Edward so stubborn, so unfeeling before' (Austen p.200). Mrs. Jennings re-situates: 'he has acted like an honest man!' (Austen p.201). John astonished but does not wish to offend anybody of good fortune. Instead notes 'extraordinary character' of Edward's behavior in light of his mother's sudden preference for brother Robert — preference 'every conscientious, good mother, in like circumstances, would adopt' (Austen p.201). Reader knows: John is upwardly malleable, Edward's mother cruel, Mrs. Jennings 'interested' though 'sincere'-coinciding with story's end (n.34: Jens Lloyd thanks).

Secondary characters establish perceived abnormality and affective reference points (regret, horror, outrage). Even more backgrounded: tertiary characters like Willoughby's obscure servant holding his horse's reins; places like Barton Cottage; legal arrangements / inheritance guidelines structuring the novel around abnormalities and local negotiation (n.35: Alex Woloch 'Character Insecurity in Austen's Sense and Sensibility' — Hegelian relative value; absolute value no longer inheres in objects but emerges in juxtaposition).

Mary Wollstonecraft in 1792 identifies the 'equivocal humiliating situation' setting women like the Dashwoods on their journey: dependent on brother John's benevolence whose marriage sets them at odds legally and emotionally. Long block-quote (n.36: Wollstonecraft Vindication 1988 Norton p.65): girls weakly educated, dependent on bounty of brothers; docile female under brother tolerable till brother marries; then wife sees her as intruder; equally-weak minds/bodies suffer in such situations — unable to work, ashamed to beg; wife cold-hearted, jealous of kindness shown her husband's relations, recourse to cunning. 'It is as if Wollstonecraft is describing the Dashwood situation exactly.'

'Wollstonecraft is critically devastating as she, like Austen, ties sensibility directly to circumstances that appear in this case recalcitrant. At the same time these circumstances reveal themselves as negotiable, ultimately, because they appear so petty and unfair.' Apparent unshakable virtues/vices (benevolence/cold-heartedness) cannot be credited solely to people — they are variables of patriarchy. Both Wollstonecraft and Austen are 'skilled negotiators as Kahneman might describe them' — showing victim's fate is not normal, alternatives easily imaginable, blame redistributed from suffering sisters to would-be benevolent brothers and petty wives. Austen's trick: characterize through people, not institutions. Wollstonecraft can foreground law/education; Austen carefully focalizes around Mrs. John Dashwood as jealous wife.

outline.function: occasion vs character — Austen quote (p.5) + closing thesis
outline.summary: Wife's cold-heartedness 'can't be attributed to bad character primarily, but only secondarily.' Austen: 'Mrs. John Dashwood had never been a favourite with any of her husband's family; but she had had no opportunity, till the present, of shewing them with how little attention to the comfort of other people she could act when occasion required it' (Austen p.5). Austen 'wonderfully cautious about distributing responsibility so that character behavior appears circumstantial, but not inevitable.' Circumstances overcome only by extraordinary sensibility for humanity — 'uncommon feeling' — 'In "Mrs. Dashwood's situation, with only common feelings," unpleasantness is to be expected' (Austen p.5). In Wollstonecraft + Austen, 'virtuous sentiments appear regrettably abnormal; the norm is vicious.'

Wollstonecraft writes in 'a disciplinary form we would now consider social science.' Such situations and the mixed feelings they engender 'deserve a certain kind of rhetorical analysis that can, indeed must, cross disciplines to do its work adequately. No single discipline has a monopoly on how norms are established referentially, and measured. At the same time we should see how rhetoric cannot be ancillary to knowledge in the disciplines, the mere linguistic form into which content is poured. In an age where the limits of rationality are newly interesting across disciplines, rhetoric is rediscovered at their very heart.' (n.37: Reddy on Paxtun marriage situations + ambivalence as nodal point of instability).

concepts.gloss: Volume's titular Ch.4 concept. Against the Galenic disequilibrium / recipe / blending-algorithm view (parts gratitude + parts happiness + dash of resentment), mixed feelings are 'a matter of negotiated circumstances where feelings may be at odds as they converge on character.' For Kahneman, ambivalencies referencing multiple points subject to negotiation or persuasion.

Gross's positive thesis: feelings 'converge on character' under socially-negotiated reference values, not as internal proportional mixings. Replaces Galen's humours model and Ekman's basic-emotions-blend model.

The long tradition (back to Galen's humours, with afterlife in Renaissance medicine — n.1: Paster, Humoring the Body 2004) that treats mixed feelings as proportional internal mixtures of stable basic elements. Gross's primary polemical target. Encompasses 'recipe' folk-psychology and homeostatic emotional-stability formula.

Austen's 'stylistically congenial' double negative — 'Not no feelings' — captures the negotiated/non-quantifiable character of mixed feelings. Operates as resistance to crass-utilitarian halving and to physiognomic legibility. Cf. half-mind idioms ('I FEEL NOT HALF BAD,' 'I HAVE HALF A MIND TO...') and aposiopesis (book p.112).

Crass utilitarianism descended from Bentham (1790s, just before Austen's epistolary 'Elinor and Marianne' draft) holds emotion and happiness quantifiable and halvable. Austen prefigures Kahneman-Tversky's prospect-theory critique: relative value (Marianne's superiority-to-Lucy retort) defeats absolute-value rational calculation (Elinor's disingenuous p.198 framing).

Gross's chapter-crux formulation, derived from Barrett + Barsalou's situated conceptualization: 'Edward's mixed feelings are defined by interested onlookers who, in this case, include us.' Onlookers (Elinor, Marianne, John Dashwood, Mrs. Jennings, Lucy, the reader) are constitutive of the feelings, not subsequent witnesses.

From Wilson-Mendenhall et al., 'Grounding Emotion in Situated Conceptualization' (2011 Neuropsychologia). Emotions are not stereotypically triggered brain mechanisms but emerge through situational conceptualization; same incentive yields different brain profiles (social fear → dlPFC/IFG; physical fear → motor).

Barrett-Barsalou's term: people 'automatically see Jim Webb as either angry or elated' depending on situational framing, 'even though sufficient information for this judgment is not unambiguously displayed on his face or body.' Provides experimental warrant for Gross's anti-physiognomic reading of Edward's astonishment.

From Kahneman's 1992 Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes article 'Reference Points, Anchors, Norms, and Mixed Feelings.' Mixed feelings indexed via 'duck/rabbit' shifts among multiple salient reference points (e.g. $3000 raise vs. zero vs. $5000-expected). Negotiators/politicians/advertisers manipulate these — labor-union lowballing, focusing illusion.

Schkade + Kahneman 1998 'Does Living in California Make People Happy?' — advertisers exploit consumer belief that change in weight, scent, etc. produces happiness improvement. Rhetorical device tying value to a 'rhetoric of possibilities.'

Famously coined by Kahneman + Tversky in prospect theory. Elinor exploits loss aversion by presenting herself as the more immediate love object while articulating the alienation that forces Edward's hand.

Austen drafted 'Elinor and Marianne' (1790s) in the wake of Bentham; Marianne's relative-value retort to Elinor's expected-utility framing prefigures Kahneman + Tversky 1979 'Prospect Theory.' Austen as proto-behavioral-economist of mixed feelings.

Mr. Bennet's astonishment scene (1833 Greatbatch engraving): astonishment renders calculation impossible because reflexive and 'all too predictable,' destabilizing emotional arc in both temporal directions; resolves only through context, not physiognomy.

anchors: n.11 (Le Brun, A Method to Learn to Design the Passions)
concepts.gloss: Charles Le Brun's classical-French Expression Studies illustrate that canonical astonishment incorporates the scalar inflection admiration and fear — astonishment 'in its unadulterated form, nothing will change per se.'

Photo of Sen. Jim Webb angry-in-isolation vs. elated-in-context. Without context: easy to mistake; cost Howard Dean the 2004 presidency. Sourced from Barrett, Lindquist, Gendron 2007 Trends in Cognitive Sciences.

Barrett's experimental finding: top-down affective information acquired through gossip influences vision — what we know about someone influences not only feeling and thinking but whether we see them at all. Provides experimental analog for John Dashwood + Mrs. Jennings as norm-setters in Sense and Sensibility.

Kahneman + Miller's Norm Theory rejects formal/informal probability conception of normality, offering instead a 'phenomenology of surprise.' Perceived abnormality + availability-of-counterfactuals modulate sympathy — Austen's plot-mechanics (the store closed for renovations, the 5-minute miss) work this way.

Gross's summary of Kahneman: 'Kahneman ties value to a rhetoric of possibilities.' Reference points are 'inillimitable' (not fixed) and subject to revision through negotiation — alternative framings ('not losing a vehicle, gaining freedom from debt').

Renaissance rhetorical figure (Peacham): 'when the truth is opposed by false terms.' Quentin Skinner's account holds it 'always possible to argue in utramque partem, on either side.' Gross uses paradiastole as the bridge concept tying classical-rhetorical reference-substitution to Kahneman's contemporary reframing-as-negotiation.

Ryle 1966 + MacIntyre 1981/2007 thesis (Gilbert Ryle 'Jane Austen and the Moralists'; MacIntyre After Virtue p.240): 'when Jane Austen speaks of happiness, she does so as an Aristotelian.' GROSS DEPARTS in n.16: 'Austenian happiness is not Aristotelian + Christian, as MacIntyre suggests' — Austen is a thorough critic of systematic thinking (utilitarian in this case).

concepts.term: EMOTIONAL STABILITY → MIXED FEELINGS → EMOTIONAL STABILITY
concepts.gloss: The folk-psychology formula characterizing Sense and Sensibility's surface arc (Dashwoods 'happily settled' in Sussex → mixed-feeling trials → 'happily resettled' in Barton/Delaford with 'strong family affection,' Austen p.289).

From Paul Goring's Rhetoric of Sensibility (2005 p.153): sentimental fiction's emotive hold over readers rests on 'the staging of witnessed eloquence that implicates a reader' + 'mechanics of the scenes in which they are depicted' — not on Lavater-style conventions of emotional expression.
Gross's synthesis of Goring + Kahneman: sentimental fiction's mixed feelings 'materialize in reference values that are negotiated only by way of rhetoric.'

Bentham's ch. VI of An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation (1780): historically-specific biases (gender, education, rank) that determine the scope of one's life; Bentham himself qualified absolute happiness models.

2005 Virtual Reality article 'Mixed Feelings: Expression of Nonbasic Emotions in a Muscle-Based Talking Head' (Fig. 4.1) — blending algorithm yields uncanny middle faces 'mathematically unhinged from implied humanity.' Visual analog of crass-utilitarian halving.
Masahiro Mori 1970s, via Wired magazine: subverted-expectations of stimuli with human/nonhuman traits — sorites-paradox explanation. Used to characterize Fig. 4.1's mathematically-blended faces.

Paul Ekman's evolutionary-psychology program — seven 'brief and episodic' emotions, with non-basic emotions as combinations/blends; mixed-emotions-on-face are likely basic emotions passing in microseconds. Gross's standing antagonist (cf. Ch.1 Darwin).
Ekman's relabeling of everything beyond his seven basic emotions — enduring emotions like love or boredom — distinguishing 'brief and episodic' basic emotions from enduring 'affective commitments.'

Cognitive Approaches to Literature (Lisa Zunshine ed., Vermeule Why Do We Care About Literary Characters?) 'frequently proceeds unecologically toward theory of mind.' Austen's withholding of omniscient narration on Edward frustrates mind-reading per se.
Ryle's 1966 'Jane Austen and the Moralists': Sense and Sensibility models Aristotelian 'equilibrium' as practical wisdom. Gross's chapter contests this reading via the disequilibrium-critique.

Wollstonecraft 1792 Vindication of the Rights of Woman: legal/economic situation of women dependent on brothers' benevolence; once brother marries, sister-in-law becomes intruder. Wollstonecraft's analytic anticipates Austen's Dashwood plot.

concepts.term: character vs. occasion (Austen's distribution of responsibility)
concepts.gloss: Austen p.5 on Mrs. John Dashwood: occasion-not-character produces the offending actions. Austen 'wonderfully cautious about distributing responsibility so that character behavior appears circumstantial, but not inevitable.' Uncommon feeling is the (unavailable) remedy.

Austen's negative-construction style — used substantively for emotional ambivalence and as resistance to physiognomic legibility; encompasses double negatives, withheld omniscience, dot-dot-dot aposiopesis.

Gross's bridge claim: even Kahneman's experimental mini-narratives are 'literary fiction... populated not with real human beings but implied human beings.' 'Scenario building — even for oneself — always relies upon narrative fictionality.' Levels Kahneman and Austen as compatibly insightful.

positions.claim: Mixed feelings are not internal proportional mixtures (Galen, Ekman, blending algorithms) but rhetorically-situated, negotiated reference values converging on character.

Ryle and MacIntyre are right that Austen 'speaks of happiness as an Aristotelian' (Ryle 1966; MacIntyre After Virtue p.240), but MacIntyre is wrong that Austenian happiness is Aristotelian + Christian. Austen is fundamentally a critic of systematic thinking — utilitarian in this chapter's case. Aristotelian background is rhetorical-pathē-tradition (via Gross's Secret History), not virtue-ethical telos.

Mixed feelings 'in the novel and beyond are poorly served by this disequilibrium model recalling the long tradition back to Galen.' Internal-proportions humours model is the chapter's primary polemical target.

Sense and Sensibility (drafted 1790s as 'Elinor and Marianne' just after Bentham) prefigures Kahneman + Tversky's 1979 prospect theory: Marianne's relative-value retort to Elinor's absolute-value framing (Austen p.198) anticipates the relative-vs-absolute psychological value distinction central to behavioral economics.

Edward's mixed feelings are 'defined by interested onlookers' (Elinor, Marianne, Lucy, John Dashwood, Mrs. Jennings, the reader) in alignment with Barrett-Barsalou's situated conceptualization: situations themselves can be ambiguous; the same incentive yields different neural/conceptual profiles depending on situated meaning.

Edward's face at the £200 scene shows only 'astonishment' — 'in its unadulterated form, nothing will change per se' — frustrating physiognomic legibility (Marianne's calculating-externalism, Lavater, Ekman). Astonishment is reflexive, predictable, scalar (Le Brun: astonishment+fear, astonishment+admiration); it obscures rather than reveals.

Austen frustrates Cognitive Approaches to Literature (Zunshine, Vermeule) by withholding omniscient narration at the crucial juncture: 'What Edward felt, as he could not say it himself, it cannot be expected that anyone else should say for him.' Mind-reading is denied at both external and internal registers.

Austen's 'stylistically congenial' double negation ('Not no feelings') is not stylistic ornament but a rhetorical-emotional device materializing the irreducible ambivalence of mixed feelings against crass-utilitarian halving.

'In an age where the limits of rationality are newly interesting across disciplines, rhetoric is rediscovered at their very heart.' Rhetoric is not 'ancillary to knowledge in the disciplines, the mere linguistic form into which content is poured' but constitutive of how norms are referentially established and measured.

Wollstonecraft (Vindication 1792) and Austen are both 'skilled negotiators' (as Kahneman would describe) who tie sensibility to circumstances that appear recalcitrant but reveal themselves as negotiable — by showing the victim's fate is not normal, alternatives easily imaginable, blame redistributed to benevolent-brothers and petty-wives. Wollstonecraft foregrounds law/education; Austen focalizes around character circumstantially.

John Dashwood and Mrs. Jennings function as 'Kahnemanite norms' — secondary/tertiary characters establish reference points beyond the central characters' purview, the 'perceived abnormality' (Kahneman + Miller 1986) that determines affective response.

tensions.description: Austen-as-Aristotelian (Ryle/MacIntyre — virtue + practical wisdom + telos of marriage in restricted households as surrogate Greek polis) vs. Austen-as-systematic-thinking-critic (Gross — Austenian happiness is NOT Aristotelian + Christian per n.16, but a thoroughgoing critique of utilitarian/calculative systematicity).

Galenic humours disequilibrium model (long tradition back to Paster's Humoring the Body) vs. Gross's negotiated-circumstances thesis — feelings as socially negotiated reference values converging on character, not as proportional internal mixings.

Ekman's basic-emotions + microsecond-passing-blends program vs. Barrett-Barsalou situated conceptualization (same face → different emotion depending on situational context, Jim Webb / Knight Dunlap fear-or-anger 'Both!').

Elinor's disingenuous expected-utility framing of Edward-marrying-Lucy (absolute-value averaging — Austen p.198) vs. Marianne's relative-value retort prefiguring Kahneman-Tversky prospect theory (loss-aversion, reference-point dependence).

Calculating externalists (Marianne; Lavater; physiognomic tradition; muscle-based talking-head blending algorithms) reading face for emotional truth vs. Gross's anti-physiognomic claim that astonishment is reflexive/predictable and only context (Mr. Bennet/Darcy/Lydia; £200/Brandon-rectory) renders feeling legible.
Cognitive-Approaches-to-Literature theory-of-mind reading (Zunshine, Vermeule) vs. Austen's calculated withholding of omniscient narration on Edward — 'he could not say it himself.'

Quentin Skinner's generic paradiastole (always possible to argue in utramque partem) vs. Kahneman's example where reference values are 'lodged in a recalcitrant world subject, however, to negotiation.' Persuasion is inillimitable BUT not unconstrained.

Dorothea Frede's reading of Aristotle's Rhetoric on mixed feelings as Phileban remedial / homeostatic (n.5) vs. Gross's identification that Aristotle uses 'mixture' vocabulary nowhere at all — situated/intentional-object framing wins out.
